prompt: On a legacy 100BASE-TX link, a server is forced to 100 Mbit/s full duplex while the switch detects the speed but uses half duplex. The link is up. Which symptoms are consistent with this duplex mismatch under bidirectional load?

options.text: The switch port logs late collisions
options.explanation: Possible. The half-duplex side detects overlapping transmissions, which can include late collisions depending on timing.

options.text: The server's NIC counts CRC errors and runt frames
options.explanation: Possible. Aborted/truncated transmissions from the half-duplex side can cause FCS/alignment or fragment counters; exact counter classification varies.

options.text: Pings succeed but large transfers are very slow
options.explanation: Possible. Light traffic may avoid overlap, while heavier bidirectional traffic exposes the mismatch.

options.text: The link fails to come up at all
options.explanation: The question explicitly states that this mismatched legacy link is up. Other negotiation/configuration failures can prevent links coming up.

workedExample: The full-duplex side can transmit while receiving. The half-duplex side treats overlapping transmissions as collisions and backs off. Error counters and heavy-load performance can reveal the mismatch even when small pings pass. Align supported settings, normally auto-negotiation on both ends; this legacy 100BASE-TX scenario does not describe every Gigabit PHY.

prompt: In a hypothetical shared half-duplex Ethernet, link rate increases but minimum frame length and collision-domain geometry stay fixed. No carrier extension is added. Why can collision detection become unsafe?

options.text: The packet's bits propagate faster whenever the link rate increases
options.explanation: The hypothesis changes the rate at which bits are sent, not signal propagation speed.

options.text: The sender remains transmitting for longer, leaving excessive collision time
options.explanation: At a higher rate the same minimum frame finishes sooner.

options.text: The sender may finish its frame before a far-end collision signal can return
options.explanation: Correct. Collision detection requires the sender still to be transmitting when the worst-case collision is heard.

options.text: The FCS becomes a MAC-level retransmission request
options.explanation: An FCS is an integrity check; ordinary Ethernet does not request retransmission after a bad FCS.

workedExample: The route's collision round-trip time stays fixed while the shortest frame's transmission time shrinks. If the sender finishes first, it can miss a late collision. Historical half-duplex Gigabit used carrier-extension symbols to address its timing model; modern full-duplex Ethernet has no shared half-duplex collision domain.

prompt: Two hosts repeatedly collide on legacy shared Ethernet. Why does binary exponential backoff widen the random waiting range after repeated collisions, up to a cap?

options.text: It guarantees that the same host always wins next
options.explanation: The waits are random; the mechanism does not guarantee a particular winner.

options.text: It reduces the chance that contending hosts repeatedly retry together
options.explanation: Correct. More possible retry times help separate contending transmissions, while carrier-sense rules still apply.

options.text: It corrects the damaged frame without resending it
options.explanation: Backoff schedules another attempt; it is not forward error correction.

options.text: It makes full-duplex Ethernet require CSMA/CD
options.explanation: Full-duplex links have no shared half-duplex collision domain and do not use this collision backoff.

workedExample: If colliding hosts always choose the same delay, they can repeat their collision. Random delays provide opportunities to separate; widening the range after failures helps when contention persists. The range is capped and attempts are limited, so this is neither a guarantee of success nor an unlimited wait policy.
